Line thickness = how critical a route is

Degree counts direct destinations; betweenness measures how often an airport is the bridge on the shortest trip between two others. They disagree most for gateway airports: Anchorage has the highest betweenness in the country with only 34 destinations. Click a row to see it on the map.

The communities

Small nationally, severe regionally

For single-airport closures: the share of one region’s airports that get cut off (colored bar) next to the share of all US trips lost (gray bar). Regions are communities with at least 20 airports. Click a bar to see that airport on the map.

Caveats. Tiny communities (3–12 airports) are left out of the regional measure, because losing one of three airports would read as 33%. Airline shares are slightly inflated by codeshare records, and small-carrier names are unreliable in OpenFlights. Alaska results inherit known gaps such as the missing Unalaska–Anchorage route.

Targeted closures break the network apart far faster than random ones. In the full network, closing Anchorage and then Seattle cuts Alaska off, which is why betweenness targeting looks so damaging; in the Lower 48 alone, degree and betweenness targeting perform about the same.

Three public sources, each doing one job: OpenFlights draws the network, BTS T-100 checks it against official route counts, and the BTS ticket survey (DB1B) supplies the travelers. All three describe 2014.

SourceWhat it containsHow this site uses it
OpenFlightsroutes.dat, June 2014 snapshot; airports.dat + airports-extended.dat Nonstop routes with the airlines that fly them; airport names and locations. No passenger counts. The network on the map: 605 airports and 2,883 routes. All critical-airport, closure, community and robustness results.
BTS T-100 Domestic Segmentall carriers, January–December 2014 Passengers, seats and flights reported by airlines for every nonstop route, every month. A check on the network: 98.9% of our routes (2,851 of 2,883) appear in T-100, and 97.5% of T-100 passengers fly routes we have.
BTS Airline Origin and Destination Survey (DB1B)Market table, April–June 2014 A 10% sample of domestic tickets: each traveler’s origin, destination and the airports they change planes at. Traveler counts in the simulator: 6.3 million sampled trips, about 1.31 million trips a day; 67% nonstop, 31% one stop, 2% two or more.

Network measures

  • A trip is a pair of open airports that could reach each other before a closure.
  • A trip is lost if no itinerary remains, and detoured if the shortest one needs more connecting flights.
  • An airport is cut off if it is no longer in the largest connected part of the network.
  • Route importance is edge betweenness: the share of shortest trips that use the route.

Traveler counts

  • Can’t travel: the trip starts or ends at a closed airport, or it connects through one and no route is left.
  • Must reroute: the trip connects through a closed airport, but another route exists.
  • Counts are travelers per day at 2014 levels (sample × 10 ÷ 91 days). Air travel is higher today.
  • Connecting matters: 49% of travelers using Atlanta and 58% using Charlotte only change planes there.

Cleaning

  • Nonstop domestic routes only; airline duplicates and codeshares merged into one link per airport pair (about 22% of pairs appear only as codeshares, so they are kept).
  • Excluded: sightseeing tours (Boulder City–Grand Canyon West, Grand Canyon–Page) and one cargo-only leg.
  • Airports missing from airports.dat (58, mostly small Alaska villages) are filled from airports-extended.dat.

Known gaps

  • OpenFlights lacks a few real routes, such as Unalaska (DUT)–Anchorage, so the Dutch Harbor and Boeing Field seaplane groups look disconnected from the start.
  • Routes that began after June 2014, such as Dallas Love Field’s long-distance flights from October, are not on the map.
  • The simulator assumes rerouted travelers find seats. Flight capacity is modeled in the separate Recovery Lab.
  • About 4% of DB1B trips are not counted: ones that start or end at an airport not on the map, or follow a very rarely flown itinerary.
  • Airline names for some small Alaska routes are unreliable in OpenFlights; the routes themselves are real.
